The Rodrigues flying fox (Pteropus rodricensis), a medium-sized pteropodid endemic to Rodrigues Island, exhibits several notable life-history traits that have been documented in both captive and wild populations. Neonates emerge at a remarkably modest size, with new-born pups weighing approximately 45 grams [Wwb = approximately 45 grams] at birth, a value that positions them among the smaller-bodied young for a fruit bat of this lineage. This low birth mass is consistent with the species' reproductive strategy of producing a single pup per litter and only one litter per year, a remarkably slow reproductive tempo. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of this species, which correspond to a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], females produce just a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], yielding a maximum annual output of only one offspring. This extremely low reproductive rate is among the lowest recorded for any Pteropus species and reflects the island's resource-limited environment.

Basal metabolic rate in Pteropus rodricensis has been measured under controlled conditions using open-flow respirometry, revealing a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 134.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 134.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This metabolic value is consistent with the moderate body size of this species, as adult females attain a maximum wet weight of 350 grams [Wwi = 350 grams], placing them at the upper end of the size range reported for the species across various field studies. The correlation between body mass and metabolic rate is well established among frugivorous bats, and this species' BMR aligns closely with predictions from allometric equations for mammals of comparable mass. Such a metabolic profile reflects the energetic demands of a relatively sedentary island lifestyle, where food resources, though seasonal, can be locally abundant. The respirometry trials were conducted during the species' active phase, ensuring that measured oxygen consumption reflected true basal conditions without the confounding effects of digestive or locomotor activity.

Gestation in the Rodrigues flying fox proceeds over a notably extended period, with pregnancy lasting approximately 198 days [tg = approximately 198 days] when females are maintained at a core body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This gestation length is considerably longer than the 120 to 180 days reported for some related Pteropus species in the literature, suggesting a comparatively slow developmental tempo that may be linked to the species' reduced metabolic rate and island habitat. The extended gestation is thought to allow for a more advanced state of neonatal development at parturition, which may enhance pup survival in an environment with unpredictable food availability. Following birth, the dependent pup undergoes a period of intense maternal investment, nursing exclusively for several months. This prolonged gestation and subsequent lactation period represent a significant energetic cost to the mother, who must maintain her own body condition while supporting the developing offspring. Field observations indicate that females prioritize pup rearing even during periods of reduced fruit abundance, underscoring the species' strong maternal commitment.

Juvenile development proceeds through several well-defined stages, beginning with a dependency phase that culminates in weaning. At the species' typical body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], weaning occurs at approximately 76 days after birth [tx = approximately 76 days after birth], a relatively brief period compared to the extended gestation, suggesting that pups undergo rapid postnatal development to achieve nutritional independence quickly. After weaning, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase characterized by continued somatic growth and behavioral maturation. Puberty, marking the onset of reproductive potential, is attained considerably later, with females reaching sexual maturity at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth] at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This one-year delay between weaning and reproductive maturity is an important life-history feature that allows young individuals to complete their growth and accumulate adequate energy reserves before engaging in the demanding process of reproduction. The extended juvenile period may also serve to reduce competition with adults for limited food resources.

Longevity records for the Rodrigues flying fox indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 28 years [am = approximately 28 years] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C], a remarkable duration for a mammal of this body size. This extended lifespan, combined with the species' extremely low reproductive output of just one pup per year, places Pteropus rodricensis at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. Such a strategy, characterized by delayed sexual maturity, prolonged gestation, and high adult survival, is typical of island-endemic species that have evolved in environments with reduced predation pressure and stable but limited resources. The trade-off between longevity and reproductive rate is particularly pronounced in this species, as individuals invest heavily in each single offspring over an extended period. This life-history pattern makes the Rodrigues flying fox particularly vulnerable to population declines from anthropogenic threats, as even modest increases in adult mortality can have disproportionately large effects on population growth rates. Conservation efforts must therefore prioritize the protection of adult females and their dependent young to maintain viable populations.
